BUSS1020 Week 03

BUSS1020 Week 03 - Basic Probability: Events, Conditional Probability, Bayes' Theorem and Counting

Overview

This week introduces the probability language and rules used whenever conclusions are drawn from data:

• Events, sample spaces, complements, simple events and joint events.

• The three approaches to probability: classical, relative frequency and subjective.

• Joint, marginal and conditional probability, and the general addition rule.

• Mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive events.

• Conditional probability, independence and the multiplication rule, shown with decision trees.

• Bayes' theorem: updating a probability when new evidence arrives.

• Counting rules: multiplication rule, repetition rule, factorials, permutations and combinations.

• The ethics of reporting probabilities.

Key Concepts

Events, sample space and complement

• A probability experiment is any process with an uncertain outcome, such as a customer responding to a survey or a product failing a quality check.

• The sample space (S) is the set of all possible outcomes of the experiment.

• An event is any subset of the sample space, for example "the customer buys the product".

• A simple event is one outcome of the experiment, for example "the customer pays by card". A joint event involves two characteristics at once, for example "the customer pays by card and is under 30".

• The complement of an event A, written A', is everything in the sample space that is not A. The complement rule is P(A') = 1 - P(A), which is often the fastest way to compute a probability such as "at least one".

• Every probability is between 0 and 1 inclusive. A probability of 0 means impossible, 1 means certain.

Three approaches to probability

• Classical probability: all outcomes are equally likely, and the probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of possible outcomes. Example: the chance of a specific face on a fair die is 1/6.

• Relative frequency probability: the probability is the proportion of times the event occurs in a large number of repeated observations. Example: 120 of 1,000 products failed a check, so the estimated failure probability is 120/1,000 = 0.12.

• Subjective probability: a degree of belief based on judgment and experience, used when outcomes are not repeatable under identical conditions, for example the chance that a new product succeeds.

Joint, marginal and conditional probability

• A joint probability is the probability that two events happen together, written P(A and B). In a two-way (contingency) table it is the count in one cell divided by the grand total.

• A marginal probability is the probability of one event alone, ignoring the other variable, written P(A). In a contingency table it is a row or column total divided by the grand total. A marginal probability is the sum of the joint probabilities across the row or column.

• A conditional probability is the probability of A given that B has occurred, written P(A | B). The condition restricts the group being considered, so the denominator is the total for B, not the grand total.

The addition rule and combining events

• General addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B). The joint probability is subtracted because the outcomes in both A and B were counted twice.

• Mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time, so P(A and B) = 0 and the addition rule simplifies to P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B). Example: a product cannot be graded both "A" and "B" in the same inspection.

• Collectively exhaustive events cover every possible outcome, so their probabilities add up to 1. The outcomes of any probability distribution must be both mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive, which is why distribution probabilities are between 0 and 1 and sum to 1.

Conditional probability, independence and the multiplication rule

• The conditional probability formula is P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B), provided P(B) > 0. The denominator is the probability (or count) of the conditioning event B.

• The general multiplication rule follows directly: P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A | B), or equivalently P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B | A).

• Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, that is P(A | B) = P(A). For independent events the multiplication rule simplifies to P(A and B) = P(A) x P(B).

• Independence and mutual exclusivity are different ideas. Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together (their joint probability is 0); independent events have no influence on each other (their joint probability is the product of their marginals). Two events that each have a positive probability cannot be both mutually exclusive and independent at the same time.

Decision trees

A decision tree maps uncertain events as branches. Each branch is labelled with a probability, and the tree is used as follows:

• Multiply probabilities along the branches of one path to get the joint probability of that sequence of events.

• Add the joint probabilities of all paths that end in the outcome of interest to get its total (marginal) probability.

• Divide the joint probability of a path by the total probability of the observed outcome to get the conditional probability (this is exactly Bayes' theorem in tree form).

Bayes' theorem

Bayes' theorem reverses a conditional probability. When P(A | B) is wanted but P(B | A) is known:

P(A | B) = P(B | A) x P(A) / P(B)

• P(A) is the prior probability of A, the belief before seeing the new evidence.

• P(B | A) is the likelihood of the evidence if A is true.

• P(B) is the total probability of the evidence, computed with the addition rule: P(B) = P(B | A)P(A) + P(B | A')P(A').

• P(A | B) is the posterior probability of A after seeing the evidence.

Counting rules give the number of possible outcomes without listing them.

Choosing k of n items, order does not matter

• Use a permutation when the arrangement matters (for example first, second and third place in a competition).

• Use a combination when only the group matters (for example a committee of 2 people chosen from 4 candidates).

• Permuting k chosen items gives k! arrangements of each combination, so nPk = nCk x k!.

Ethics of probability work

Probabilities and risks must be reported honestly and clearly: state the assumptions behind the numbers, do not present a subjective probability as if it were a measured frequency, and do not hide inconvenient outcomes. Decision-makers can only weigh risk correctly if the probabilities they are given are accurate and honestly interpreted.

Worked Examples

Joint, marginal and conditional probability: a fleet of cars

Of 500 company cars, 300 have a GPS navigation unit, 200 have air conditioning, and 150 have both.

Define the events: A = "has GPS", B = "has air conditioning". The counts are: both = 150, GPS only = 300 - 150 = 150, air conditioning only = 200 - 150 = 50, neither = 500 - 150 - 150 - 50 = 150.

Joint probability: P(A and B) = 150 / 500 = 0.30.

Marginal probabilities: P(A) = 300 / 500 = 0.60, P(B) = 200 / 500 = 0.40.

Addition rule: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A and B) = 0.60 + 0.40 - 0.30 = 0.70, which matches the count (150 + 150 + 50) / 500 = 350 / 500.

Conditional probability: P(A | B) = P(A and B) / P(B) = 150 / 200 = 0.75. Among cars with air conditioning, 75% also have GPS. Note the denominator is 200 (the cars in the condition), not 500.

Multiplication check: P(A and B) = P(B) x P(A | B) = 0.40 x 0.75 = 0.30, which agrees with step 2.

Because P(A | B) = 0.75 differs from P(A) = 0.60, having air conditioning and having GPS are not independent in this fleet.

Permutations versus combinations: choosing two letters

Choose 2 letters from A, B, C and D.

Permutations (order matters): the number of ordered selections is 4P2 = 4! / (4 - 2)! = 24 / 2 = 12. Listing them confirms it: AB, AC, AD, BA, BC, BD, CA, CB, CD, DA, DB, DC. AB and BA count as different arrangements.

Combinations (order does not matter): the number of unordered groups is 4C2 = 4! / (2! x 2!) = 24 / 4 = 6. The groups are {A,B}, {A,C}, {A,D}, {B,C}, {B,D}, {C,D}.

The two answers differ by a factor of 2 = 2!, because each pair can be arranged in 2! = 2 ways: 4P2 = 4C2 x 2! = 6 x 2 = 12.

Bayes' theorem: airport security screening

A scanner at airport security detects prohibited items. Suppose 0.1% of passengers actually carry such an item, the scanner correctly flags 99% of those who do, and it falsely flags 5% of passengers who do not. If a passenger is flagged, what is the probability the passenger really carries the item?

Define events: C = "carries a prohibited item", F = "flagged". Prior: P(C) = 0.001, so P(C') = 0.999.

Likelihoods: P(F | C) = 0.99, P(F | C') = 0.05.

Total probability of a flag: P(F) = P(F | C)P(C) + P(F | C')P(C') = 0.99 x 0.001 + 0.05 x 0.999 = 0.00099 + 0.04995 = 0.05094.

Bayes' theorem: P(C | F) = P(F | C) x P(C) / P(F) = 0.00099 / 0.05094 = 0.01943.

Interpretation: a flagged passenger has only about a 1.9% chance of actually carrying the item. Even a highly accurate test produces mostly false alarms when the event is rare, because the 5% false-positive rate applies to the very large group of ordinary passengers.

Probability from counts

If 84 of 439 observed cases fall in an event of interest, its relative-frequency probability is 84 / 439 = 0.19134, about 19.1%. The observed share is slightly below one fifth of all cases.
